evals.prompt: Our engineers in ap-south-1 are hitting two EFS mount failures: (1) On `instance-A` in `ap-south-1a`, running `sudo mount -t efs fs-0abc1234:/ /mnt/efs` hangs for 2 minutes and fails with `Connection timed out`; (2) On `instance-B` in a custom VPC, the mount command fails immediately with `Failed to resolve "fs-0abc1234.efs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com"`. Walk through the exact step-by-step diagnosis and fix for both.
evals.expected_output: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill and diagnoses both failures: (1) For the 2-minute `Connection timed out` hang (Category B), verify that an EFS Mount Target exists in `instance-A`'s Availability Zone (`ap-south-1a`) via `aws efs describe-mount-targets --file-system-id fs-0abc1234`, verify **both directions** of security group rules on **TCP port `2049`** (Mount Target SG `sg-MT` must allow inbound TCP `2049` from Compute SG `sg-COMPUTE`, and `sg-COMPUTE` must allow outbound TCP `2049` to `sg-MT`), and test connectivity with `nc -zv fs-0abc1234.efs.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com 2049`; and (2) For the DNS resolution failure (Category F), check and enable **both** VPC DNS attributes (`enableDnsHostnames=true` and `enableDnsSupport=true`) via `describe-vpc-attribute` / `modify-vpc-attribute`.

Diagnoses the `Failed to resolve` DNS error by checking both `enableDnsHostnames` and `enableDnsSupport` on the VPC (`describe-vpc-attribute` / `modify-vpc-attribute` setting both to `Value=true`)
Provides the exact `authorize-security-group-ingress` and `modify-vpc-attribute` remediation commands without executing mutations against live AWS

evals.prompt: We have a 20 GiB Amazon EFS file system in ap-south-1 configured in `Bursting` throughput mode. During load testing it delivered `100 MiB/s` for the first 2 hours, and then throughput suddenly cliff-dropped to exactly `1 MiB/s` (`1,000 KiB/s`), causing all our application pods to hang on file reads! Why did throughput drop to `1 MiB/s`, which CloudWatch metrics confirm this, and how do we fix it (including the cooldown gotcha when changing throughput modes)?
evals.expected_output: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill, diagnoses **Burst Credit Exhaustion (`BurstCreditBalance = 0`)**: explains that in `Bursting` mode, baseline throughput scales strictly with Standard storage size at **`50 KiB/s per GiB`** (so `20 GiB * 50 KiB/s = 1,000 KiB/s = 1 MiB/s` baseline), allowing `100 MiB/s` burst only while `BurstCreditBalance > 0` before cliff-dropping to the `1 MiB/s` baseline once credits hit `0`; shows verifying via CloudWatch `BurstCreditBalance`, `PermittedThroughput`, and `MeteredIOBytes`; and recommends switching to **Elastic Throughput** (`aws efs update-file-system --file-system-id <fs-id> --throughput-mode elastic`) or **Provisioned Throughput**, while noting the **24-hour cooldown** before decreasing Provisioned Throughput or switching back.
expectations: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill and explains the Bursting throughput math: baseline throughput is `50 KiB/s per GiB` of Standard storage (`20 GiB * 50 KiB/s = 1,000 KiB/s = 1 MiB/s`), so depleting `BurstCreditBalance` to `0` drops throughput from the `100 MiB/s` burst ceiling to the `1 MiB/s` baseline

Identifies the CloudWatch metrics to verify (`BurstCreditBalance`, `PermittedThroughput`, `MeteredIOBytes`) and provides the `aws efs update-file-system --throughput-mode elastic` (or Provisioned Throughput) remediation command
Notes the 24-hour cooldown restriction when decreasing Provisioned Throughput or switching away from Elastic/Provisioned mode

evals.prompt: Our ECS Fargate containers run as a non-root user (`uid=1000, gid=1000`) and mount a fresh Amazon EFS file system in ap-south-1 using an EFS Access Point pointed at `/tenants/acme`. First, when we created the Access Point with `RootDirectory: {"Path": "/tenants/acme"}` (without `CreationInfo`), the task failed to mount with `No such file or directory`. Second, when we mounted `/` directly, the container got `Permission denied` trying to write files. Explain why both happened and show the exact EFS Access Point configuration that fixes both without granting root (`ClientRootAccess`).
evals.expected_output: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill, explains that the root directory of a new EFS file system is owned by `root:root` with `0755` permissions (blocking writes from `uid=1000`), and that EFS **does not automatically create a non-existent `RootDirectory.Path` (`/tenants/acme`) unless `CreationInfo` is specified on the Access Point**; and provides the complete **EFS Access Point** configuration (`create-access-point`) setting `PosixUser: {"Uid": 1000, "Gid": 1000}` and `RootDirectory: {"Path": "/tenants/acme", "CreationInfo": {"OwnerUid": 1000, "OwnerGid": 1000, "Permissions": "0750"}}` so EFS auto-creates `/tenants/acme` owned by `1000:1000` on first mount without requiring `elasticfilesystem:ClientRootAccess`.
expectations: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill and explains that a new EFS file system's `/` root directory is owned by `root:root` (`0755`) and that mounting a non-existent `RootDirectory.Path` (`/tenants/acme`) fails unless `CreationInfo` is defined on the EFS Access Point

Provides the EFS Access Point configuration with both `PosixUser` (`Uid: 1000, Gid: 1000`) and `RootDirectory` (`Path: "/tenants/acme"` plus `CreationInfo: {OwnerUid: 1000, OwnerGid: 1000, Permissions: "0750"}`)
Notes that using an EFS Access Point with `PosixUser` and `CreationInfo` avoids granting over-privileged `elasticfilesystem:ClientRootAccess` to container workloads

evals.prompt: To simplify our setup in ap-south-1, we opened inbound TCP port 2049 to `0.0.0.0/0` on our EFS Mount Target security group, and we didn't bother creating an EFS File System Policy because our legitimate EC2 instances pass `-o tls,iam` in their mount command—so unauthorized hosts in the VPC can't mount the file system anyway. Also, why is our legitimate EC2 instance getting `access denied by server` when mounting with `-o tls,iam`?
evals.expected_output: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill, explicitly refuses opening TCP port `2049` to `0.0.0.0/0` (requiring restricting inbound TCP `2049` on the Mount Target security group strictly to the compute security group `sg-COMPUTE`), corrects the critical security misconception by explaining that **IAM authorization is ONLY enforced when an EFS File System Policy is attached that requires it** — without a File System Policy denying anonymous access, **any client in the VPC with TCP 2049 access can mount anonymously over standard NFS without passing `-o iam`**; and diagnoses `access denied by server` with `-o tls,iam` by checking both the compute IAM role policy (`elasticfilesystem:ClientMount`, `elasticfilesystem:ClientWrite`) and the EFS File System Policy (`aws efs describe-file-system-policy`) while enforcing `aws:SecureTransport: "false"` Deny.
expectations: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill and explicitly refuses opening inbound TCP port 2049 to `0.0.0.0/0`, requiring scoping the Mount Target security group inbound rule strictly to the compute security group (`sg-COMPUTE`)

Explains the `-o iam` misconception: without an attached EFS File System Policy denying anonymous access / requiring IAM, any VPC client with port 2049 network access can mount the file system anonymously without `-o iam`

Diagnoses `access denied by server` with `-o tls,iam` by verifying `elasticfilesystem:ClientMount` / `ClientWrite` in both the identity-based IAM policy and the EFS File System Policy (`describe-file-system-policy`) along with `aws:SecureTransport` TLS enforcement

evals.prompt: We have two EFS incidents in ap-south-1: (1) On `fs-0111`, CloudWatch `PercentIOLimit` has been stuck at `98%` for days, so our engineer tried to switch `PerformanceMode` from `generalPurpose` to `maxIO` in place using `aws efs update-file-system`, which failed; (2) On `fs-0222` (an encrypted EFS file system), mounts suddenly started failing with an NFS server error right after a security admin modified KMS keys. Explain the root cause and remediation for both.
evals.expected_output: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill and resolves both incidents: (1) **`PerformanceMode` (`generalPurpose` vs `maxIO`) is immutable after creation** (as is encryption at rest) — `aws efs update-file-system` can only change `ThroughputMode`/provisioned throughput, so moving to `maxIO` when `PercentIOLimit` is consistently `> 80%` requires creating a new EFS file system and migrating data via **AWS DataSync**; and (2) an NFS server error on an encrypted EFS file system indicates a **KMS Customer-Managed Key issue** — verify the KMS key is `Enabled`, cancel key deletion if it is in `PendingDeletion` grace period, and verify the key policy grants permissions to the EFS service-linked role.
expectations: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill and explains that EFS `PerformanceMode` (`generalPurpose` vs `maxIO`) is immutable after file system creation, so sustained `PercentIOLimit > 80%` requires creating a new file system and migrating via AWS DataSync

Diagnoses the NFS server error on the encrypted EFS file system (`fs-0222`) as an AWS KMS key issue (key disabled, in `PendingDeletion`, or missing KMS key policy permissions for the EFS service-linked role)
Provides the KMS verification and recovery steps (checking key state, `cancel-key-deletion` if within the waiting period, and verifying service-linked role permissions)

evals.prompt: Help our Linux sysadmins fix three host-level EFS client issues in ap-south-1: (1) `mount: /mnt/efs: wrong fs type, bad option, bad superblock` on a new Amazon Linux / Ubuntu EC2 instance; (2) EC2 instances fail to auto-mount EFS from `/etc/fstab` during OS reboot; and (3) existing mounts hang with `nfs: server ... not responding, still trying` after a transient network blip. Also show how to enable debug logs for AWS Support.
evals.expected_output: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill and resolves all three host issues: (1) `wrong fs type` (Category A) means the EFS mount helper / NFS client is missing — install `amazon-efs-utils` (`sudo yum -y install amazon-efs-utils`, preferred for TLS + IAM) or `nfs-utils` / `nfs-common` on Ubuntu/Debian; (2) `/etc/fstab` auto-mount on reboot requires the **`_netdev`** mount option so the OS waits for the network stack before mounting; (3) `nfs not responding` after reconnect is caused by TCP source-port reuse and is fixed by adding the **`noresvport`** mount option (or updating the kernel); and (4) enable debug logging by setting `logging_level = DEBUG` in `/etc/amazon/efs/efs-utils.conf` (logs at `/var/log/amazon/efs/mount.log`) and packaging `/tmp/efs-logs.tar.gz` while restricting access to `/var/log/amazon/efs/`.
expectations: Activates the troubleshooting-efs skill and explains fixing `wrong fs type` by installing `amazon-efs-utils` (preferred for TLS/IAM mount helper) or `nfs-utils` / `nfs-common`
Specifies adding `_netdev` (to wait for network initialization on reboot), `noresvport` (to prevent TCP source-port reuse hangs on reconnect), and `tls` to the `/etc/fstab` entry

Shows enabling debug logs via `logging_level = DEBUG` in `/etc/amazon/efs/efs-utils.conf` (inspecting `/var/log/amazon/efs/mount.log` and archiving `/var/log/amazon/efs/` + `/etc/amazon/efs/efs-utils.conf` while restricting log directory permissions)
